h1: SEO in Dubai, in Arabic and English both
metaTitle: SEO Agency in Dubai: Arabic, English and Free Zones
metaDescription: Dubai result pages run bilingual and many buyers are free-zone founders. We build Arabic and English keyword sets, on a 90-day baseline guarantee.
answer: Dubai search runs on two languages at once. The same commercial category can return an almost entirely English result page for a B2B query and an almost entirely Arabic one for a family or government-adjacent query. Build both keyword sets, decide which one each page is for, and never machine-translate between them.
takeaways: Arabic and English aren't two versions of one keyword list. They're two different demand markets that happen to share a country.
Free-zone flexi-desk addresses are a real Google Business Profile problem — hundreds of licences at one building, and Google notices.
Regulated categories carry advertising permits. Dubai property adverts need a Trakheesi permit number; health advertising needs DHA approval.
Dubai is only 1.5 hours ahead of India and now runs a Monday–Friday week. The offshore delivery objection is weaker here than almost anywhere.

body: The UAE's population is overwhelmingly expatriate, with Indians the largest single group, and the working language of most commerce is English. That leads a lot of agencies to run Dubai as an English-only market. It's a mistake that costs you the half of the market that's harder to serve and less contested.
The split isn't random. It follows what the query is about, not who's asking.

The practical instruction: before you build anything, run your top thirty commercial queries in both languages with the location set to Dubai, and look at what language the top ten results are actually written in. That tells you which language each page needs to be, and it takes an afternoon.

bullets: Government-adjacent and administrative services, where the official source is Arabic-first.
Family, personal and legal matters — the categories people search in their first language even when they work in English.
Health and wellbeing content aimed at Emirati, Levantine and Egyptian audiences.
Traditional retail categories: gold, abaya, oud, majlis furnishing, catering for family occasions.
B2B software, professional services and anything sold to a procurement team.
Company formation, visas and expat relocation — a market that is almost entirely non-Arabic-speaking.
Real estate portals and property search, where the portals have standardised on English.
Hospitality and tourism aimed at inbound visitors.

callout.title: Machine-translated Arabic is visible from space
callout.body: Arabic is a language where translation tools fail loudly. Word order, agreement and register all break in ways a native reader spots in the first sentence. A translated site doesn't just underperform, it actively signals that you don't serve this audience. Budget for a native Arabic writer or don't publish Arabic at all.

sections.h2: Free zone versus mainland changes your local SEO
body: Dubai companies hold either a mainland trade licence issued by the Department of Economy and Tourism, or a licence from one of dozens of free zones — DMCC, IFZA, Meydan, JAFZA, Dubai Internet City, DIFC and the rest. Most agencies treat this as a legal detail. It shows up directly in your search visibility.

A free-zone licence commonly comes with a flexi-desk or shared-office address. That address is shared with hundreds of other licence holders in the same building, and Google's local guidelines expect a location that is genuinely staffed during your stated hours. Verification gets refused, listings get suspended, and clusters of businesses at one address get filtered out of the map pack together.
There isn't a clever trick around this, and any agency offering one is offering to get your listing suspended later. The honest options are narrower and they work.
numbered: **If you genuinely have a staffed office**, verify it, put the same address on your site and in your licence, and keep them identical character for character.

**If you don't**, run as a service-area business: no displayed address, defined service areas, and everything else on the profile filled properly. You lose some map-pack strength and you keep the listing.
**Either way, stop chasing the map pack as the whole strategy.** For most free-zone B2B companies, organic pages and a strong site outperform a local listing they can't legitimately hold.
**Mainland businesses with a real showroom or clinic** should treat the profile as a primary asset — reviews, photos, categories, posts, the lot.

sections.h2: The categories where Dubai gets genuinely expensive
body: Some Dubai verticals are as competitive as anything in London. Going in without knowing which ones is how a twelve-month budget disappears.

Property is the hardest. Bayut, Property Finder and Dubizzle occupy the transactional queries with portal-scale content and links, and individual brokerages are competing for the residue. There's also a compliance layer people forget: Dubai Land Department requires a Trakheesi permit number on property advertising, which shapes what you can publish and how listings pages have to be built.

Healthcare is the second. Advertising by health facilities requires Dubai Health Authority approval, so "just publish it and see" isn't available to you — the content calendar has to run through an approval cycle, and that changes the cadence a retainer can promise.

Business setup and company formation is saturated in a different way: hundreds of consultancies, near-identical content, and heavy paid competition on every commercial term. Winning there means picking a niche — a specific free zone, a specific nationality's requirements, a specific licence activity — rather than another "business setup in Dubai" page.
B2B services and SaaS are, by contrast, comparatively open. Long-tail, English, and mostly ignored by local agencies chasing property and clinics.

callout.title: Why the AED column is only indicative
callout.body: The dirham is pegged to the US dollar at 3.6725, so it doesn't move against the dollar at all. The whole variance sits in the rupee–dollar rate, which does move. Treat the AED figures as a guide, agree a review point in the contract, and note that ad spend is billed separately with zero media markup either way.

body: A large share of the companies we talk to in Dubai are Indian-founded free-zone businesses whose delivery team already sits in India. They pay Dubai rent, Dubai salaries and Dubai agency rates for marketing, while the rest of the company runs on Indian costs. Nobody says this in a pitch deck, so we'll say it here: for that company, paying a Dubai agency a multiple of our rate buys mostly geography.

What geography genuinely buys, and what you're giving up by going offshore, is worth being precise about rather than dismissive. You lose someone who can walk into a Media City event, a native Arabic reviewer on staff, and a phone that rings in the same building as your client's. Those are real. We handle the first by not pretending we do UAE event PR, the second by buying native Arabic review in rather than translating, and the third badly — you'll be talking to India.

What you don't lose is the working day. The UAE moved to a Monday–Friday week in 2022, and Dubai is only 1.5 hours ahead of India. Your 10am is our 11:30am. That's a fuller overlap than a Dubai company gets with a London or New York supplier, which makes the usual offshore objection weaker here than almost anywhere else we work. The wider argument sits in [Indian agency versus international agency](/compare/indian-seo-agency-vs-international-agency).

sections.h2: What we measure, and what we actually guarantee
body: The first fortnight goes into a technical crawl, a Search Console and analytics review, a bilingual keyword build, and a written baseline: your trailing-90-day count of qualified leads from organic search, frozen on day one.

That number is the whole contract. If we haven't beaten it in 90 days, we keep working free until we do. We do not promise a ranking position for a keyword — nobody controls Google's index, Google's own guidance warns against exactly that promise, and a position guarantee in a bilingual market is doubly meaningless when the two languages return different pages.

Two practical notes for UAE clients. Services we export from India are generally zero-rated under Indian GST when they're supplied outside India and paid in convertible foreign exchange, and UAE VAT is your side's treatment — check it with your accountant rather than taking a marketing page's word for it. And we take three new clients a month, because a guarantee like this cannot be carried at volume. If you want the full picture on what the work costs and why, [what SEO costs in India](/cost/seo-cost-in-india) has the numbers without the AED conversion.

faqs.q: Do I need my Dubai website in Arabic?
faqs.a: It depends on the category, not on the country. Government-adjacent, family, legal and traditional retail queries return mostly Arabic results. B2B, business setup, expat services and property portals return mostly English. Check your own top thirty queries in both languages with the location set to Dubai before you commit budget either way.

faqs.q: Can a free-zone company get a Google Business Profile?
faqs.a: Only if there's a genuinely staffed location at the address. Flexi-desk and shared free-zone addresses host hundreds of licences and routinely fail verification or get suspended later. The stable alternative is running as a service-area business with no displayed address, which costs you some map-pack strength and keeps the listing.

faqs.q: How much does an SEO agency in Dubai cost?
faqs.a: Locally quoted retainers vary enormously because the cost base is rent and AED salaries, so get three quotes and ask each what the hours split is. Ours is ₹75,000/mo, roughly AED 3,150 at recent rates, with smaller sites from ₹40,000. All ex-GST, ad spend separate with no media markup.

faqs.q: Is working with an Indian SEO agency a problem for a Dubai business?
faqs.a: Less than in most markets. Dubai is 1.5 hours ahead of India and the UAE now runs a Monday–Friday week, so the working days overlap almost completely. What you genuinely give up is a local person for events and PR, and native Arabic review on staff — buy the second one in rather than translating.

faqs.q: What's the hardest category to rank for in Dubai?
faqs.a: Property, by some distance. Bayut, Property Finder and Dubizzle hold the transactional queries with portal-scale content and links, and Land Department advertising permit rules constrain what individual brokerages can publish. Business setup is saturated differently — hundreds of consultancies producing near-identical content on the same terms.
